code.originalText: Diagnosis of mismatch repair-deficient low rectal cancer: staging, tumor board plan, medical oncology and colorectal surgery consultation, genetic counseling, and the start of PD-1 blockade

text.paragraph: Diagnosis visit: biopsy and staging results, the tumor board plan, and the oncology and surgical consultations. [S]

Ms. Didrikson Zaharias returns two weeks after her first visit. Colonoscopy three days after that visit found an ulcerated mass in the lower rectum, from 4 to 9 cm from the anal verge, and nothing else in the colon; the biopsies show adenocarcinoma, and the tumor has lost the mismatch repair proteins MSH2 and MSH6 and is microsatellite instability high. Rectal-protocol MRI shows a tumor whose lower edge is about 1 cm above the anorectal junction, growing just through the bowel wall, with two suspicious lymph nodes and a clear mesorectal fascia (cT3bN1). CT of the chest, abdomen and pelvis shows no spread. The tumor board met three days ago. She was seen today by Dr. Albright-Nakamura and by the colorectal surgeon, who explained that surgery for a tumor this low would most likely mean removing the rectum and anus with a permanent colostomy. She still passes some bright red blood most days, less than before, and feels tired on the back nine. Her first question was whether she would need a bag; her second was whether she could keep playing. [S]

list.item:
Low rectal adenocarcinoma, mismatch repair deficient, cT3bN1M0 (C20). Rectal cancer diagnosed two weeks after she first came, because the bleeding in a woman of 41 was examined and scoped at once rather than treated as hemorrhoids. It is locally advanced and low, so standard treatment would be chemoradiation and chemotherapy followed, in most cases, by an abdominoperineal resection and a permanent colostomy. Because the tumor is mismatch repair deficient, the tumor board and Dr. Albright-Nakamura recommend PD-1 blockade with dostarlimab for six months instead, which in the published trials has given a clinical complete response in nearly every patient with this kind of tumor and allowed the rectum to be kept, without radiation or surgery. She agreed, with the understanding that chemoradiation and surgery remain available if the response is not complete. [S]
Dostarlimab 500 mg every three weeks from next week, nine doses.
Hepatitis B, hepatitis C and HIV tests drawn today; urine pregnancy test negative today.
Germline multigene panel sent after counseling today.
Restaging MRI, sigmoidoscopy and rectal examination after four doses.

Iron deficiency anemia from rectal blood loss (D50.0). Hemoglobin 11.1 g/dL today (11.0 at the first visit, with ferritin 9 ng/mL); oral iron was started once the results had been reviewed; bleeding continues but is lessening. [S]
Ferrous sulfate 325 mg every other morning.
Blood count in four weeks; ferritin at three months.

Rectal bleeding with a change in bowel habit and a rectal mass (K62.5). Explained by the diagnosis made today; superseded. [S]
Problem resolved.
